Bad timing to build new — both GPUs and RAM are in a genuine price spike right now, not just normal fluctuation. Here's what's actually happening and three real options with current numbers.

**Why it's ugly right now**
- DDR5 has roughly quadrupled since mid-2025 — a 32GB kit that was ~$100-200 is now $350-650+. AI datacenter demand for HBM memory is eating the DRAM wafer capacity that used to make consumer RAM.
- RTX 4090 (discontinued, no more made): $2,500-3,700 street price, more than double its $1,599 MSRP.
- RTX 5090 (current flagship): MSRP was $1,999, but it's trading $3,000-4,000+ right now for the same shortage reasons.
- RTX 3090 used (24GB, last-gen): the one component that hasn't moved much — still $800-1,100, because it's not being newly manufactured and the 5090's high price has propped up its resale value.

**Three real builds**

1. **Budget — single used RTX 3090 (24GB VRAM)**
   Card ~$900 + AM5 budget CPU/board ~$350 + 32GB DDR5 ~$380 + 850W PSU ~$120 + case/NVMe ~$150 → **~$1,900 total**. Runs 30B models comfortably, 70B at tight quantization. This is the only tier that isn't badly distorted by the shortage.

2. **Mid — dual used RTX 3090 (48GB VRAM combined)**
   Two cards ~$1,800 + better platform for PCIe lanes ~$500 + 64GB DDR5 ~$650 + 1200W PSU ~$200 → **~$3,300-3,600 total**. Comfortable 70B inference, some headroom for larger context.

3. **Sidestep the shortage entirely — Mac Studio**
   Apple's unified memory isn't subject to the same GPU/DRAM spot-market chaos since it's baked into a fixed SKU price. M4 Max, 128GB: ~$3,500-4,000 configured, runs 70B models at full quality, ~150W power draw. M3 Ultra 96GB starts at $5,299. Note Apple cut the 512GB tier this year — if you need more than 96-128GB unified memory, your only current option is the new M5 Ultra Mac Studio (512GB config not shipping until late October 2026, base M5 Ultra starts $5,499).

**My actual read**: tier 1 (single 3090) is the only build that makes financial sense right now — new-GPU and new-RAM builds are paying a shortage tax that won't reliably pay off in performance. If you need more than 24GB VRAM, the Mac Studio route is currently a better dollar-per-usable-GB than a dual-3090 PC once you account for how DDR5 pricing also inflates the PC build's non-GPU costs.

Why DDR5 Prices Have Nearly Quadrupled in 2026

A 32GB DDR5 kit that cost around $95 to $250 in mid-2025 is now running $550 to $650, and some forecasters don't think the ceiling has been hit yet. Dell and Lenovo have both moved to raise hardware prices in response. Buyers who assumed this was a normal supply blip are finding out it isn't. The DDR5 shortage driving these prices has a specific, traceable cause: HBM (high bandwidth memory), the memory format powering AI accelerators, is eating the wafer capacity that used to go to standard DDR5 DRAM.

Fusion Worldwide's Market Research Manager, Andrew Czuczwa, flagged a forecast update that shows this squeeze getting worse before it gets better. Here's the story behind the price spike, in plain terms, and what it means for anyone sourcing DDR4 or DDR5 memory right now.

 

Industry Insider Episode 6: Why DDR5 Prices Quadrupled in 2026
Youtube

 

Key Takeaways


Standard DDR5 memory prices have risen sharply through 2026, with some 32GB kits climbing from roughly $95 to $250 in mid-2025 to $550 to $650 today, driven by DRAM capacity shifting toward HBM.
HBM's share of global DRAM wafer production has grown to an estimated 23% in 2026, up from about 8% in 2024, as manufacturers chase far higher HBM margins.
HBM memory demand forecasts across all three major manufacturers just rose from 34 exabytes to 40 exabytes, a jump analysts expect to correspond to a 22-exabyte shortfall in DDR5 DRAM, since one HBM wafer consumes the equivalent of 3 to 4 normal DDR5 wafers.
Because memory makers are allocating capacity to HBM first, buyers sourcing DDR4 and DDR5 should expect longer lead times and tighter allocation through the rest of this year and into next.

A Price Spike With a Different Cause

Past DRAM shortages, like the ones in 2017-2018 and 2021, were cyclical. Manufacturers underbuilt capacity, demand spiked, and supply eventually caught up.

What’s left still beats a single consumer GPU on capacity โ a 96GB Ultra loads a 70B at Q8 that no 24GB card can touch โ but the “run any frontier model locally” pitch died with the high-memory SKUs. If you need more than 96GB in 2026, no Mac desktop provides it; the only 128GB Mac is the M5 Max MacBook Pro.

The M3 Ultra is essentially two M3 Max chips fused together via UltraFusion โ double the cores, double the memory bandwidth. What is the best LLM to run on Mac Studio?
Mac Studio M4 Max (128GB): Qwen 3 32B at full BF16 (~35 tok/s), Llama 3.3 70B at Q4 (~20 tok/s). Mac Studio M2 Ultra (192GB) handles even larger models. For coding: Qwen 2.5 Coder 32B.
How much faster is Mac Studio vs Mac Mini for LLMs?
Mac Studio M4 Max is 2-3× faster for large model inference (400GB/s bandwidth vs 273GB/s). More importantly, 128-192GB unified memory enables 70B+ models that don't fit on Mac Mini's 64GB max.
Is Mac Studio M4 Max worth it for local AI?
Yes — 128GB unified memory handles 70B models at full quality without quantization trade-offs. At $1,999 for the base M4 Max (128GB), it's competitive with a dual-RTX-3090 PC build for the same VRAM capacity.
Can Mac Studio run vision models locally?
Yes — LLaVA, Qwen VL, and Llama 3.2 Vision all run via Ollama on Mac Studio with Metal acceleration. 128GB Mac Studio runs the 90B vision model smoothly.

Bad timing to build new — both GPUs and RAM are in a genuine price spike right now, not just normal fluctuation. Here's what's actually happening and three real options with current numbers.

**Why it's ugly right now**
- DDR5 has roughly quadrupled since mid-2025 — a 32GB kit that was ~$100-200 is now $350-650+. AI datacenter demand for HBM memory is eating the DRAM wafer capacity that used to make consumer RAM.
- RTX 4090 (discontinued, no more made): $2,500-3,700 street price, more than double its $1,599 MSRP.
- RTX 5090 (current flagship): MSRP was $1,999, but it's trading $3,000-4,000+ right now for the same shortage reasons.
- RTX 3090 used (24GB, last-gen): the one component that hasn't moved much — still $800-1,100, because it's not being newly manufactured and the 5090's high price has propped up its resale value.

**Three real builds**

1. **Budget — single used RTX 3090 (24GB VRAM)**
   Card ~$900 + AM5 budget CPU/board ~$350 + 32GB DDR5 ~$380 + 850W PSU ~$120 + case/NVMe ~$150 → **~$1,900 total**. Runs 30B models comfortably, 70B at tight quantization. This is the only tier that isn't badly distorted by the shortage.

2. **Mid — dual used RTX 3090 (48GB VRAM combined)**
   Two cards ~$1,800 + better platform for PCIe lanes ~$500 + 64GB DDR5 ~$650 + 1200W PSU ~$200 → **~$3,300-3,600 total**. Comfortable 70B inference, some headroom for larger context.

3. **Sidestep the shortage entirely — Mac Studio**
   Apple's unified memory isn't subject to the same GPU/DRAM spot-market chaos since it's baked into a fixed SKU price. M4 Max, 128GB: ~$3,500-4,000 configured, runs 70B models at full quality, ~150W power draw. M3 Ultra 96GB starts at $5,299. Note Apple cut the 512GB tier this year — if you need more than 96-128GB unified memory, your only current option is the new M5 Ultra Mac Studio (512GB config not shipping until late October 2026, base M5 Ultra starts $5,499).

**My actual read**: tier 1 (single 3090) is the only build that makes financial sense right now — new-GPU and new-RAM builds are paying a shortage tax that won't reliably pay off in performance. If you need more than 24GB VRAM, the Mac Studio route is currently a better dollar-per-usable-GB than a dual-3090 PC once you account for how DDR5 pricing also inflates the PC build's non-GPU costs.

chat_messages.text:
Because "server" isn't a hardware spec — it's a job description. Any machine running server software (file sharing, Plex, a database, a web app) that other devices connect to over the network is functioning as a server, regardless of what it looks like.

A "real server" (Dell PowerEdge, HP ProLiant) is built with server-specific hardware: ECC memory, redundant power supplies, hot-swap drive bays, remote management, hardware meant to run unattended 24/7 for years. A mini PC is just a small consumer computer — same CPU/RAM/storage architecture as a laptop — that someone installed server software on and left running in a closet.

Both do the job. The difference is durability and features, not function:
- Mini PC as server: cheap, quiet, low power, but consumer-grade parts, no redundancy, no ECC RAM to catch memory errors.
- Purpose-built server: built to run hot 24/7 without dying, has actual server management features, costs more and draws more power/noise.

So when people say "mini PC that qualifies as a server," they mean it's small and cheap but you're using it *as* a server — same way a laptop running a website is technically "a web server" even though nobody would call a laptop server-grade hardware.

# The TrueNAS 180TB Budget Beast

Building an Enterprise-Grade NAS on a budget in 2026

Hard drive prices are starting to come down for the first time since March of 2025. If you've wanted to build a NAS but storage costs were too high, 2026 is officially the year of the **Budget Beast**. By leveraging refurbished enterprise gear and ECC RAM, you can achieve data center reliability without the $10,000 price tag.

[![Dell Precision 5820](https://i.ebayimg.com/images/g/x3kAAeSwlrFpeaVB/s-l1600.webp)](https://www.ebay.com/itm/336409897375?mkcid=1&mkrid=711-53200-19255-0&siteid=0&campid=5339149544&toolid=80006&mkevt=1)

## [Dell Precision 5820 Tower](https://www.ebay.com/itm/336409897375?mkcid=1&mkrid=711-53200-19255-0&siteid=0&campid=5339149544&toolid=80006&mkevt=1)

$229.88

The foundation of our build. This is enterprise-grade hardware featuring a **Xeon W2123** and **64GB DDR4 ECC RAM**. This machine is built to run 24/7 without breaking a sweat.

- Always change BIOS to "Power on automatically after power loss."
- Setup OS to run on 2x 2.5" SSD in Raid 1 for redundancy.
- Needs a [second 1TB SSD](https://amzn.to/4cMzzt9) ($80+).
- Mount easily with the [Icy Dock 2-bay Adapter](https://amzn.to/3QGCmvm) ($34.95).

**PRO TIP:** Check the listing for the **950W version**. It's safer for high-drive counts and 10GbE network cards for future expansions of your homelab, it's addicting!

[![Highpoint RocketStor 6438TS](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/I/61C5rbbfaBL._AC_SL1500.jpg)](https://www.amazon.com/Highpoint-RocketStor-6438TS-Hot-Swappable-Enclosure/dp/B0BT423JTB)

## [Highpoint RocketStor 6438TS 8-Bay Enclosure](https://www.amazon.com/Highpoint-RocketStor-6438TS-Hot-Swappable-Enclosure/dp/B0BT423JTB)

$599.00

This JBOD tower is the key to our mass storage. It features **SFF 8644 ports**, which allows for direct, lightning-fast connection to your server.

**WARNING:** The included RAID card is not a true HBA. Sell it on eBay and use the Broadcom card below for ZFS support.

You will also need [2x SFF 8644 cables](https://amzn.to/4cxNG4r) to complete the link.

[![LSI 9300-8e HBA](https://i.ebayimg.com/images/g/ZqcAAOSwuhRjdGbD/s-l1600.jpg)](https://www.ebay.com/itm/134329871174?mkcid=1&mkrid=711-53200-19255-0&siteid=0&campid=5339149544&toolid=80006&mkevt=1)

## [Broadcom LSI SAS 9300-8e (IT Mode)](https://www.ebay.com/itm/134329871174?mkcid=1&mkrid=711-53200-19255-0&siteid=0&campid=5339149544&toolid=80006&mkevt=1)

$49.88

This is the gold standard for TrueNAS. It's pre-flashed to **IT Mode**, giving ZFS direct access to your drives. Reach out to seller *jiawen2018*-they are excellent and very helpful with HBA needs.

[![18TB SAS Drive](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/I/51ZW0CvzEhL._AC_SL1200_.jpg)](https://amzn.to/4t8VtN2)

## [18TB Seagate SAS Drive (Renewed)](https://amzn.to/4t8VtN2)

$365.55

18-20TB drives are the current "sweet spot." Renewed drives come with a 1-year warranty and SAS drives are built to last a lifetime. Buy an extra spare with the savings and always run at least **Raid-Z1**.

![QNAP Enclosure](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/I/81D32P4g8EL._AC_SL1500.jpg)

### Avoid the QNAP Trap

The [QNAP TL-D800S ($724.06)](https://amzn.to/4mu5h1w) might look easier, but it has severe limitations for a serious server:

- **No SAS Support:** The enterprise SAS drives mentioned in this article WILL NOT WORK in this QNAP.
- **Proprietary RAID:** You're paying extra for a card that isn't a true HBA.
- **Stability:** USB/SATA bridge connections are notoriously unstable compared to SFF-8644 for hosting applications.

content.text:
This is the actual answer to what you asked — max storage, real hosting capability, minimum price. The trick is: don't buy a NAS box. Build a DAS setup around cheap enterprise gear, because right now hard drives are the *one* storage component that hasn't been hit by the AI shortage — HDD prices are up "only" ~2.45x year over year vs SSD's 6.5x, and bulk enterprise HDDs are sitting flat around $17-25/TB.

**The build (verified current pricing):**

- **"Brain" — Dell Precision 5820 Tower**: $230. Xeon W2123, 64GB DDR4 ECC already installed. This is your compute/hosting layer.
- **8-bay DAS enclosure — Highpoint RocketStor 6438TS**: $599. This is what actually gives you the storage density — connects via SAS, not USB.
- **HBA card — Broadcom LSI 9300-8e (IT mode)**: $50. Gives ZFS/TrueNAS raw access to every drive, no proprietary RAID nonsense.
- **Cables + boot mirror SSDs**: ~$150 (SFF-8644 cables + a mirrored boot pair for redundancy).
- **Storage — 8x 18TB enterprise SAS drives**: $365 each = $2,924. That's 144TB raw.

**Total: ~$3,950** for a system with 144TB raw storage, ECC memory throughout, and a real Xeon to run things on.

**With RAIDZ2** (survives 2 drive failures, which you want for anything you can't afford to lose): **~108TB usable**.

**Hostability**: run TrueNAS SCALE (free) on it — it does ZFS storage AND runs apps/containers/VMs natively, so Plex, Nextcloud, a Docker stack, whatever — same box.

**Want it cheaper?** Same formula, half the drives: 4x 18TB ($1,462) instead of 8, RAIDZ1, ~54TB usable, total system ~$2,470.

**Avoid**: off-the-shelf NAS boxes (QNAP etc.) — SATA-only, proprietary RAID emulation instead of real ZFS, and you pay more per TB for worse hardware.
